message.content: <local-command-caveat>Caveat: The messages below were generated by the user while running local commands. DO NOT respond to these messages or otherwise consider them in your response unless the user explicitly asks you to.</local-command-caveat>

<local-command-stdout>Set effort level to high (saved as your default for new sessions): Comprehensive implementation with extensive testing and documentation · burns fastest — medium handles most tasks</local-command-stdout>

Gemini issues
Prod: 404 "Publisher model ... locations/us-central1/... gemini-3.8-flash was not found"
Symptom: Gemini calls fail in production with a 404 naming locations/us-central1. The same code works on localhost.

Cause: gemini-3.8-flash is only served on Vertex AI's global endpoint, not in us-central1. Localhost has GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global in .env.local. In prod, at least one container does not see that value, so src/lib/env.ts falls back to its default, us-central1.

The service-account key is not the problem: the error names the right project, so auth worked.

src/lib/gemini/client.ts is the only place that creates the Gemini client, and @google/genai uses exactly the location we pass. So us-central1 can only come from the container's environment or the default in src/lib/env.ts.

Fix 1: code default (needs a contract: commit; src/lib/** is frozen)
In src/lib/env.ts:

-  GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION: z.string().min(1).catch('us-central1'), // blank line in .env also falls back
+  GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION: z.string().min(1).catch('global'), // blank line in .env also falls back
Commit it on its own, titled e.g. contract: default GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION to global, together with the SPEC.md env table default (us-central1 → global), and drop "Set to global" from that row and the README's "set GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global" steps if you want them optional, then merge and deploy (./deploy.sh on the server).

Optional, to see what each container actually uses: in getClient() in src/lib/gemini/client.ts, right after the client is created, add:

console.info(`[gemini] vertex project=${env.GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT} location=${env.GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION}`);
Then check docker compose logs web | grep gemini.

.env.example and the README already say to set global. Also change the fallback in scripts/gemini-smoke.mjs to global in the same commit (it mirrors src/lib/env.ts so the smoke test catches a missing setting).

Fix 2: check the server (works without a deploy)
On the VPS:

cd ~/hackcamp27
# Must print exactly GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global$ once. ^M$ = Windows line endings, a second line = duplicate (last one wins).
grep -n "GOOGLE_CLOUD" .env.production | cat -A
# Fix Windows line endings if needed:
sed -i 's/\r$//' .env.production
# Every web replica must print global:
for c in $(docker compose ps -q web); do docker exec "$c" printenv GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION; done
# env_file is only read when a container is created, so recreate after any change:
docker compose up -d --force-recreate web
Also check for other places that could set it: .env next to docker-compose.yml, or exported shell variables (env | grep GOOGLE).

Local dev reminders
Sign in: gcloud auth application-default login and gcloud auth application-default set-quota-project <PROJECT_ID>.
.env.local needs GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=<PROJECT_ID> and GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION=global (required until Fix 1 is merged). If you copied an older .env.example, it may still say us-central1: change it.
Smoke test: node --env-file=.env.local scripts/gemini-smoke.mjs. implement these fixes for the gemini 404 in production when you search for recipe

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact can declare — calling the user's claude.ai connectors (MCP) from the page, and future abilities. Load this BEFORE passing `capabilities` to the Artifact tool or writing any `window.claude.mcp` code.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

# Mise

A hands-free cooking companion: scan pantry items, find recipes that match what you have and your diet, then cook with gesture/voice control. Built with Next.js (App Router), Auth0, Postgres/Tigerdata, Gemini, MediaPipe, and ElevenLabs TTS.

Full product spec, data model, and API contracts live in [`SPEC.md`](./SPEC.md).

## Prerequisites

- Node.js >= 22 (`node -v`)
- npm
- [Google Cloud CLI](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install) (`gcloud --version`), used to sign in to Vertex AI for Gemini
- Access to the team's Google Cloud project: ask the project owner to grant your Google account the **Vertex AI User** role (`roles/aiplatform.user`)

## Setup

```bash
npm install
```

This also runs `scripts/copy-assets.mjs` (`postinstall`), which copies the MediaPipe and zxing WASM binaries into `public/` so the browser loads them locally instead of from a CDN.

### Environment variables

```bash
cp .env.example .env.local
```

Fill in the values (ask a teammate for the shared Auth0, database and barcode keys). See `SPEC.md` §8 for the full list.

### Gemini (Vertex AI)

Gemini runs on Vertex AI with Application Default Credentials (ADC), so there is no Gemini API key. Each developer signs in with their own Google account:

```bash
gcloud auth application-default login
gcloud auth application-default set-quota-project <PROJECT_ID>
```

Then set `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=<PROJECT_ID>` in `.env.local` (`GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` defaults to `us-central1`). Check it works with:

```bash
node --env-file=.env.local scripts/gemini-smoke.mjs
```

### Database

```bash
npm run migrate
```

## Running locally

```bash
npm run dev
```

Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000).

- Cook mode can run against fixtures by setting `NEXT_PUBLIC_COOK_FIXTURES=true`.
- `/api/tts` uses ElevenLabs when `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` is set; without it, voice falls back to the browser's built-in speech.

## Deployment

Production runs with `docker compose up -d --build` on the VPS. The server can't sign in through a browser, so it uses a service-account key:

1. Create a service account with the **Vertex AI User** role and download its key as `gcp-sa.json`.
2. Copy it next to `docker-compose.yml` on the server (`chmod 600`). It is gitignored; never commit or share it.
3. Put `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` in `.env.production`. `docker-compose.yml` mounts the key and sets `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`.

## Other scripts

```bash
npm run lint       # eslint
npm run typecheck   # next typegen + tsc --noEmit
npm run test        # vitest
npm run build        # production build
npm run start         # serve production build
```

## Project structure

- `src/app` — routes (App Router): landing page, `(app)` shell (Today, Pantry, Recipes, Cook, Settings, Onboarding), API routes.
- `src/features` — client-side feature logic: `cook`, `gesture`, `voice`.
- `src/contracts` — shared domain/API types and fixtures used across workstreams before real endpoints land.
- `src/components/ui` — shared UI primitives.
- `src/lib` — server-only helpers (auth, db, etc. as they're added).
- `public/models`, `public/mediapipe`, `public/zxing` — gesture/vision model and WASM assets.

## Team workflow

This repo uses [Entire](./CLAUDE.md) for branch/trail-based review on top of Claude Code. See `CLAUDE.md` for the exact workflow, and `hang.md` / `jerry.md` / `johnny.md` for each workstream's task breakdown.
